title: How engineers built a car that steers with its wheels
subtitle: Two layers: a reference model and a PID decide how much the car should rotate, a QP allocator decides which wheels pay for it. The checks ask whether each layer does its job, whether the tires were saturated enough for any of it to matter, and whether the result survives the numbers it was built on.
findings: The two-layer controller works as advertised: the allocator delivers the demanded yaw moment to within 60.23 N.m, and yaw-rate tracking error through the corner falls 88%.

It is worth +5.2% of cornering limit, +0.69% of the corner section and +0.51% of the whole lap — the last number is small because 260 of the lap's 393 m are a power-limited straight where a yaw controller has nothing to do.
On the skidpad, which is what the ~9% published figure measured, it is worth +1.30% of sustained lateral acceleration.
About 40% of the gain is the allocator alone, with its yaw demand forced to zero. Most of what a torque-vectoring system buys on this lap is not torque vectoring.

The number depends on the driver as much as on the car: across a +/-30% change in how far ahead the SAME driver looks, the gain runs from -0.34% to +11.55%. A controller is tuned against a driver whether or not anyone says so.
The passive limited-slip differential is the slowest configuration tested (14.719 s against the open differential's 14.508 s), which is Episode 12's push-wide appearing in a lap time.

checks.name: the_allocator_delivers_the_moment_it_is_asked_for
checks.detail: across the whole lap the largest gap between the moment the PID asked for and the moment the four wheels produced is 60.2 N.m, against a peak demand of 996 N.m — 6.0% at the worst instant of the lap and near zero for the rest of it. The lower layer is almost never the limitation: the tires have longitudinal capacity to spare nearly every time they are asked, and what shortfall there is comes from the allocation being computed once per control interval on the previous instant's loads, which is what a real ECU has to do.
checks.group: Does the controller reach the wheels at all?

checks.name: the_upper_layer_tracks_its_reference_better_than_the_passive_car
checks.detail: RMS yaw-rate error against the same reference model, through the same corner at the same aggression: passive 0.1662 rad/s, controlled 0.0197 rad/s (88% lower). This is what the controller was built to do, and it is a more direct measurement of it than any lap time.
checks.group: Does the controller reach the wheels at all?

checks.name: the_car_was_driven_at_the_limit
checks.detail: the quickest valid TV lap peaks at 0.969 g against a measured steady-state ceiling of 0.951 g, and reaches 9.9 deg of slip where the tire's peak at this load is near 10.4 deg. Torque vectoring only acts where tires are saturated, so a result measured with an under-driving car measures nothing — this check is the precondition for every number in this episode.
checks.group: Were the tires saturated enough for it to matter?

checks.name: no_quoted_lap_left_the_tire_fit
checks.detail: every lap quoted anywhere in this episode stayed inside the +/-12 deg region the tire file was fitted over. Laps outside it are discarded, not celebrated (rule 4), and they are discarded one lap at a time (F70).
checks.group: Were the tires saturated enough for it to matter?

checks.name: torque_vectoring_raises_the_cornering_limit
checks.detail: the passive car runs out of road above grip_use 1.041; the controlled one holds on to 1.095, +5.2%. Same driver, same line, same speed plan — the only difference is which wheels got which force.

checks.name: the_gain_is_below_the_best_published_figure
checks.detail: on the skidpad — the manoeuvre the ~9% figure comes from, and the most favourable one there is — this controller is worth +1.30% of sustained lateral acceleration. The 9% is an OUTSIDE number (rule 2) and it is a ceiling: our model does not get to beat the most favourable published case, and if it did that would be a bug rather than a result. **The citation is outstanding**: the figure comes from this project's own series plan, which states it without a reference, so it is marked as needing one rather than presented as verified (rule 2's own instruction about unsourced bands).

checks.name: the_passive_limited_slip_differential_is_slower_than_an_open_one
checks.detail: the LSD's best valid lap is 14.719 s against 14.508 s for the open differential, and its cornering limit is 0.969 against 1.041. This is Episode 12's push-wide (F76/F77) showing up in a lap time for the first time: a locking device drags the outside wheel and yaws the car out of the corner, and here that costs the driver the corner entry.

checks.name: the_control_condition_separates_the_two_layers
checks.detail: the allocator with its yaw demand forced to zero reaches 1.063 against the open differential's 1.041 and the full controller's 1.095. So 40% of the improvement is the LOWER layer alone — spreading brake and drive force across four wheels in proportion to what each has left — and only the remainder is yaw control. A study without this condition would have attributed all of it to torque vectoring. Across the sensitivity runs the share spans 38-56%, so this is a 'roughly half' claim rather than a decimal one — but the ordering open < allocator < full controller holds in every one of them.
checks.group: Is it the yaw control, or just better bookkeeping?

checks.name: on_the_skidpad_the_allocator_alone_buys_nothing
checks.detail: sustained lateral acceleration: open 0.939 g, allocator-only 0.932 g, full controller 0.951 g. On a steady circle there is no braking to distribute and almost no drive force to spread, so the lower layer has nothing to be clever with and lands slightly BELOW the passive car — the whole skidpad gain is yaw control. The same two layers therefore split the credit completely differently in the two manoeuvres, which is an argument for reporting the decomposition per manoeuvre rather than once.
checks.group: Is it the yaw control, or just better bookkeeping?

checks.name: the_conclusion_survives_plus_or_minus_3_percent_of_track_width
checks.detail: track width is the moment arm for torque vectoring and is only [LIKELY] (CLAUDE.md). At -3% the gain is +5.36% and at +3% +5.00%, against +5.18% nominal. The magnitude moves with the arm, as it must; the conclusion does not.
checks.group: Does the conclusion survive the numbers it rests on?

checks.name: the_conclusion_survives_the_driver_being_tuned_differently
checks.detail: **This check is expected to fail, and the failure is the finding.** The driver's preview time is [ASSUMED], and it is exactly the unstated protocol choice rule 9 was written about. Nominal gain +5.18%. At 30% LESS preview it is -0.34% — the passive car improves to 1.057 and the controlled one falls to 1.054, a difference of 0.0036 in grip_use against a bisection resolution of 0.002, so it is barely more than nothing rather than a reversal. At 30% MORE preview the gain is +11.55%. **The measured value of the controller therefore varies by more than the controller is worth, depending on how the driver it is helping was tuned** — and the threshold is not being loosened to hide that (F69).
checks.group: Does the conclusion survive the numbers it rests on?

checks.name: the_conclusion_survives_the_allocator_s_priority_ratio
checks.detail: when the two demands cannot both be met the allocator has to prefer one, and the preference is a modelling choice. Weighting the moment 4x gives +5.18% and weighting it 1/4 gives +4.66%.
checks.group: Does the conclusion survive the numbers it rests on?

checks.name: the_disturbed_comparison_has_enough_samples_to_be_a_rate
checks.detail: 40 seeded laps per configuration with steering noise, not repeats of one (F66) and not the ten that produced a retracted conclusion in Episode 11 (F70).
checks.group: Does it help a driver who is not perfect?

checks.name: what_the_disturbance_study_found
checks.detail: open diff: 40/40 valid, 14.59 +/- 0.00 s · LSD: 0/40 valid, nan +/- nan s · allocator only: 40/40 valid, 14.60 +/- 0.00 s · TV (4 wheels): 40/40 valid, 14.57 +/- 0.00 s · TV (rear axle): 40/40 valid, 14.59 +/- 0.00 s — all at grip_use 0.991.
checks.group: Does it help a driver who is not perfect?

checks.name: the_two_headline_numbers_are_not_independent
checks.detail: Lap time and cornering limit are the same measurement twice: every configuration drives the same plan, so a quicker lap is only available by surviving a more aggressive plan. They are both reported because a lap time is legible and a grip_use is not.
checks.group: Does it help a driver who is not perfect?

checks.name: magnitudes_are_not_quotable
checks.detail: Rung 2 (rule 15). Four independently commanded wheel forces is an electric car, not RV-1. Track width is [LIKELY] and is the moment arm. The driver is a centreline tracker, not a racing driver, so it cannot trade line for exit and its absolute lap times are not comparable with the optimal-control episodes (rule 6). Ordering and direction are the result.
checks.group: Does it help a driver who is not perfect?
